# The Peeking Problem 

Sources: 
- [Is Bayesian A/B Testing immune to peeking? Not exactly](http://varianceexplained.org/r/bayesian-ab-testing/)
- [How Not to Run an A/B Test](https://www.evanmiller.org/how-not-to-run-an-ab-test.html) 

Say you are a data scientist running an A/B test on a new feature. Let's say you run this experiment for 20 days, and on each day get 10,000 samples. Further, suppose that the groundtruth is that for both version A and version B, the clickthrough rate^[A typical definition for Clickthrough rate (CTR) is clicks $\div$ impressions (number of times the ad is shown). See [this page](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/2615875?hl=en#:~:text=Clickthrough%20rate%20(CTR)%20is%20a%20ratio%20that,*%20Ads%2C%20listings%2C%20and%20keywords%20are%20performing) for details. ] is 0.1%. We can simulate the total number of clicks during a single day as following a Binomial distribution. 

Let's say we use the Chi-squared two sample proportion test. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# set random seed 
set.seed(57)
# simulate daily clicks 
clicks_A_daily <- rbinom(20, size = 10000, prob = 0.001)
clicks_B_daily <- rbinom(20, size = 10000, prob = 0.001)
# calculate cumulative clicks 
clicks_A_cum <- cumsum(clicks_A_daily)
clicks_B_cum <- cumsum(clicks_B_daily)

impressions_cum <- (1:20) * 10000

# loop and calculate p-value for each day 
p_values_cum <- numeric(20)

for (d in 1:20) {
  k_A <- clicks_A_cum[d]
  k_B <- clicks_B_cum[d]
  n_total <- d * 10000
  
  observed_data <- matrix(
    c(k_A, n_total - k_A,
      k_B, n_total - k_B), 
    nrow = 2, 
    byrow = TRUE
  )
  
  test_result <- chisq.test(observed_data, correct = FALSE)
  
  p_values_cum[d] <- test_result$p.value
}

# p_values_cum
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df <- p_values_cum %>% as_tibble() %>% 
  mutate(day = 1:20)

df %>% ggplot(aes(x = day, y = value)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, color = "red")
```

![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


If we simply decided to stop collecting data on day 3 or day 4, then we probably would never realize that in the long run, the p-value is indeed not statistically significant. 

We can repeat the above experiment for 100 times: 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
# define function for simulation 
sim_one_day <- function(i){
  # simulate daily clicks 
  clicks_A_daily <- rbinom(20, size = 10000, prob = 0.001)
  clicks_B_daily <- rbinom(20, size = 10000, prob = 0.001)
  # calculate cumulative clicks 
  clicks_A_cum <- cumsum(clicks_A_daily)
  clicks_B_cum <- cumsum(clicks_B_daily)
  
  impressions_cum <- (1:20) * 10000
  
  # loop and calculate p-value for each day 
  p_values_cum <- numeric(20)
  
  for (d in 1:20) {
    k_A <- clicks_A_cum[d]
    k_B <- clicks_B_cum[d]
    n_total <- d * 10000
    
    observed_data <- matrix(
      c(k_A, n_total - k_A,
        k_B, n_total - k_B), 
      nrow = 2, 
      byrow = TRUE
    )
    
    test_result <- chisq.test(observed_data, correct = FALSE)
    
    p_values_cum[d] <- test_result$p.value
  }
  
  p_values_cum %>% as_tibble(.) %>% 
    mutate(day = 1:20, 
           exp_id = i)
}

total_sim_df <- data.frame()

for (i in 1:100){
  total_sim_df <- rbind(total_sim_df, sim_one_day(i))
}
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Warning in chisq.test(observed_data, correct = FALSE): Chi-squared
approximation may be incorrect
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
total_sim_df <- total_sim_df %>% group_by(exp_id) %>% 
  mutate(ever_sig = any(value <= 0.5)) %>% 
  ungroup(.)

total_sim_df %>% group_by(ever_sig) %>% count(.)
```

Hmm the above graph looks a bit weird ... 

Anyways, the promise that the frequentist paradigm is making is that it helps control the type I error. When executed correctly. Bayesians don't help with this. 

If we do want to do things correctly and not let's say, run an experiment for an indefinite amount of time, another thing to do is to implement (frequentist) sequential Bayesian testing correctly. 

:::{.callout-note}
## Does Bayesian A/B Testing solve the problem of peeking^[aka "optional stopping"]? 

The short answer is no. See explanations [here](https://www.alexmolas.com/2025/10/30/bayesian-ab-test-peeking.html) and [here](http://varianceexplained.org/r/bayesian-ab-testing/). 

There is also this [research paper](https://alexdeng.github.io/public/files/continuousMonitoring.pdf) on optional stopping in Bayesian testing. 
:::

# Some reflections 

I think the real thing underlying all of this is that they each contain their baked in assumptions, and it is important that we know which assumptions to use and which not to use.
